Born and raised in northeastern Massachusetts, the congressman graduated from Harvard in 2001 with a degree in physics. He joined the Marines days after graduation and only a few months before 9-11. He served four tours in Iraq, two as a platoon commander and two as a special assistant to General David Petraeus. Seth led a frontline infantry platoon in the first Marine company to enter Baghdad and later worked to establish a free and independent Iraqi media. He acted as a liaison to senior Iraqi military and political leaders. He was an outspoken critic of the Iraq war, but he nonetheless served his country with honor and left the Marines in 2008 with the rank of captain. He was twice decorated for valor in Iraq, a fact he kept hidden from even his parents until it was later reported by the Boston Globe. After returning home from Iraq, Seth used the GI Bill Restoration Act to earn joint degrees in business and public administration, also from Harvard. He then served as managing director of Texas Central, the company that is building the first Hyde speed rail line in Texas. The Afghan army fought for their country's freedom for two decades despite facing overwhelming odds.
It is morally imperative to continue questioning the decisions surrounding the Afghanistan withdrawal.
Withdrawing U.S. support abruptly removed critical capabilities essential to the Afghan army’s effectiveness.
A large-scale humanitarian crisis now exists in Afghanistan following the U.S. withdrawal.
Some argue that maintaining a small troop presence in Afghanistan would have required escalation due to anticipated Taliban offensives.
The rapid takeover by the Taliban raises serious military and strategic questions about the effectiveness of training efforts.
Millions of Afghan girls currently cannot attend school due to the Taliban's restrictions.
Many Americans, including veterans and political figures across party lines, wish to avoid discussing the war in Afghanistan.

assumptions.text: Continued engagement in Afghanistan requires sustained material and military support; without it, local forces cannot sustain operations.
Moral responsibility toward Afghans extends beyond immediate withdrawal and includes ongoing concern and action.
Future U.S. military engagements depend on credibility built through consistent commitment and follow-through.
Public memory and discourse shape national values and foreign policy legitimacy over time.
Americans value national pride and prefer narratives of success rather than prolonged conflict or failure.
The willingness of allies to cooperate militarily hinges on trust in U.S. reliability and consistency.
Military training that mirrors Western standards creates dependency on external resources and infrastructure.
Young people have a civic duty to engage with national challenges and contribute meaningfully to society.
Veterans’ emotional investment in the war implies a personal stake in its legacy and public understanding.
Educational institutions play a key role in shaping ethical citizenship and long-term societal reflection.
